newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle crew finishing orbital research.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle crew finishing orbital research.

text.p: Crew members of the space shuttle Discovery finished testing a Japanese prototype robot arm on Friday and took a last look at Comet Hale-Bopp as they neared the end of their orbital research.

"The mission has been going great," shuttle commander Curt Brown said. "We've completed eight days of very intense payload operations. It's going to be one of the shuttle missions we can look back on and be very, very proud of."
A 5-foot-long (1.5-metre) Japanese robot arm got an extra workout on Friday to complete tests that were delayed because of computer and communications glitches on Wednesday.
The $100 million mechanical marvel is slated to tend to experiments and equipment mounted on the exterior of a Japanese laboratory module in the proposed International Space Station.
Although the arm's orbital workouts during the mission were frequently stalled by an oversensitive safety system and other minor problems, the astronauts said they were pleased with its performance.
"I'd give it an A-plus," astronaut Jan Davis said. "It's really been fun. We sort of feel like test pilots up here trying out the arm."
Mission control celebrated the successful checkout of the arm by playing the astronauts "Mr. Roboto" by Styx.
"If we weren't dancing before, we certainly are now," astronaut Steve Robinson said. "We are celebrating here tonight by eating curry rice."
The astronauts on Friday also focused their 7-inch (18-cm) ultraviolet telescope on the receding Comet Hale-Bopp for a fourth and final look at the gases and dust spewing from its icy body.
Astronomers hope data from the telescope will help them learn more about the cosmic ingredients that formed the solar system.
The ozone-monitoring satellite that has trailed Discovery since being released from the shuttle last week was due to be picked up on Saturday.
The shuttle will swoop in and grab the German-built spacecraft at about 11:16 a.m. EDT (1516 GMT), testing a maneuver needed for space station dockings.
Much of the data taken during a nine-day checkup on the health of Earth's upper atmosphere has been recorded aboard the spacecraft, and scientists are eager to see the results.
Discovery is scheduled to end its 11-day mission on Monday with a landing at Florida's Kennedy Space Center.
